extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literature, social critics, and writers interested in literary aesthetics and social influence
extracted.subtask_description: An essayistic literary-criticism subtask examining how 'parlor-mindedness' (private, decorous social norms) shapes taste, conversation, art, and moral life; useful for writers and critics deciding what subjects, tone, and audiences literature should address. Focuses on social and aesthetic consequences rather than technical craft rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parlor as 'talking room' but limits discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: The parlor is 'a place for social intercourse' and 'a talking room,' yet in practice it confines conversation to limited, safe topics (kitchen, nursery, dressmaker's shop) rather than broader ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues we should expect social spaces to foster 'interchange of thought' about art, politics, science, and the moving thoughts of the world. It criticizes the parlor for producing 'shop-talk mostly, gossip of the daily concerns of the speakers,' thus stunting intellectual life and social growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free, fluent social interchange as a desideratum
rubrics_metrics.description: Social contact should be 'fluent and free, spontaneous, natural' so that people 'go as they are drawn to those who feed us best.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay presents free exchange as essential to 'the growth of thought' and the replenishment of the 'social battery.' It recommends meeting in varied contexts (work, studio, business office) to reveal true character and stimulate thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parlor-mindedness narrows literary taste (no controversy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parlor-mindedness yields a canon of literary judgment that excludes controversy: 'Pleasant if possible, or sweetly sad, and not provocative of argument--this is the demeanor of the parlor table.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because 'controversy has no place in parlors,' editors and writers conform to a menu of safe reading; the writer 'must submit' to readers' decisions. The essay implies a critical criterion: literature should resist parlor pressure and be willing to provoke argument and tackle controversial subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artists should not cater solely to parlor tastes
rubrics_metrics.description: Art that merely 'suits the uses of that carpeted sanctuary' (portraits of agreeable young ladies, decorations for parlors) is limiting; great art is 'largely conceived, largely executed' for public or monumental contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns that when parlor tastes dominate patronage, artists are forced to paint what suits domestic decoration rather than large public works; thus artists should aim for wider, bolder conceptions rather than parlor-friendly trivialities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value the voices of lesser artists/works
rubrics_metrics.description: The poem 'The Minor Birds' asks whether lesser voices (lark, thrush, blackbird) should be silenced because of the nightingale, arguing implicitly that minor voices deserve to be heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to literary judgment: do not elevate a single great voice to the exclusion of many small, joy-giving voices; recognize and preserve 'the small songs of nesting, pairing, wooing' alongside masterpieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic sense must extend beyond private parlors to public spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Confined parlor taste makes people indifferent to 'the ugliness of our town or city, schoolhouse or street-car'; a true sense of beauty should inform public institutions and spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay gives practical examples (blackboards could be restful deep red or somber green) and argues that mothers' parlor tastes should not blind them to the need for public art and better-designed schools and streets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parlor etiquette teaches exclusiveness and falsehood to children
rubrics_metrics.description: Children observing parlor conventions learn exclusiveness and the 'white lie'—polite concealments and artificial steering away from undesirable topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a normative point for social and literary depiction, the essay highlights how parlor manners inculcate falsehood and narrow social circles, thereby shaping characters and social mores that writers and critics should recognize and challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtship and intimate knowledge require everyday contexts, not parlors
rubrics_metrics.description: Parlors produce 'parlor manners' and 'parlor topics' that obscure real character; to know a person truly one should meet them in working clothes and ordinary life, not only in parlors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For fiction and social commentary, the essay recommends depicting and encouraging meetings in studios, workshops, and offices to reveal authentic habits and character—courtship confined to parlors yields superficial unions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid veiling life’s realities; literature should face naked truths
rubrics_metrics.description: Parlor-mindedness drapes 'veil on veil' over birth, death, and other salient life-processes, making them remote and symbolic; the parlor does not admit 'naked truths.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author urges confronting real facts of life in speech and art rather than cloaking them in polite euphemisms; this is an evaluative standard for serious literature and social discourse.
